title: The Battle of the Camel
hookLine: Aisha, Talhah and Zubayr oppose Ali, and believers fight believers

cards: A camel stands in the middle of a battlefield outside Basra. On its back is a covered litter, and inside is Aisha, the Prophet's widow, the woman Muslims call a mother of the believers.
Around the camel, men are dying to protect it. Facing them is the army of Ali, the Prophet's cousin. With Aisha are Talhah and Zubayr, two companions the Prophet had promised paradise.
Every name on this field belongs to the Prophet's own circle. That is what makes the day so hard to tell.

teach.b: How did it come to this? Uthman's killers were still among the crowds. Aisha, Talhah and Zubayr demanded that justice for his blood come first.

Ali held that the state had to be steadied before the guilty could be found and punished. Both sides wanted justice for Uthman; they disagreed about the order. Aisha's party went to Basra, and Ali followed.
The histories say talks went far and a settlement seemed close, and then fighting broke out, some reports say in the night, stirred up by men who feared any peace would expose them.
Bukhari keeps a moment from just before.
Ammar ibn Yasir, on Ali's side, stands in the pulpit at Kufa and says of Aisha: she is the wife of your Prophet in this world and the next, but God is testing you, whether you will obey Him or her.
Even from the other side, Ammar would not speak of her without honor. The Qur'an had already named this kind of day.
In Pickthall's translation: "And if two parties of believers fall to fighting, then make peace between them." The verse does not say one side stops being believers. Ali's army won.
The histories say Ali sent Aisha back to Medina with honor and an escort.
Sunni teaching holds that the companions on both sides acted on their best judgment, and honors them all. Shia Muslims hold that Ali was in the right and that those who fought him erred.
Your line holds what both sides grieve.

how: Sunni Muslims teach the Battle of the Camel as a tragedy among honored companions who acted on their judgment; Shia Muslims teach it as Ali's rightful defense of his caliphate. Both recite the verse on making peace between two parties of believers.

games.q: you're Ammar, on Ali's side, speaking to the people of Kufa about Aisha, who leads the other side. what do you say?
o: she is the Prophet's wife in this world and the next, but this is a test.
games.why: Bukhari reports Ammar honored her as the Prophet's wife in both worlds, and called the day a test of whom they would obey.

practice: Bring to mind a place where Muslims are divided right now: a country, a city, a mosque committee, a family. You don't need to know who is right; hold both sides in mind at once, honored people on each.
If you pray, ask God in your own words to make peace between them, as the verse asks of believers; if you don't, simply wish them peace.

wordCard.voice: Ammar, who stood with Ali's army at Kufa and still called Aisha the wife of the Prophet in this world and the next. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the day of the camel, the name the histories give the battle.

carryVoice: Your line: believers against believers. Honor can cross the lines, as Ammar's did. See you tomorrow.
